The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. Persistence overview describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.

The second operation is reading the key. A browser can expose an object whose `getItem` later throws. `readPreferences` protects that call and returns `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` on failure. Its optional call also accommodates a `null` store. A successful read can return no value, a malformed string or valid preferences; those are separate outcomes from a thrown read.

The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.

These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.

## What the current fallback preserves

Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.

After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.

If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.

An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.

## No implicit retry service

The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

Corrupt data policy follows the rejection branches in detail. Storage quota notes explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. Storage testing guide extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Import safety policy
This page explains how Neon Pairs validates untrusted exchange text before a browser session or replay result can use it.

The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.

## Field diagnostics and the current implementation

A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.

The implementation already rejects extra keys, but does not yet produce that field-specific notice. `hasExactKeys` returns a boolean, `decodeSnapshot` returns `null`, and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures. `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. The current adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field as the diagnostic policy requires.

The existing code does not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. Its boolean exact-key helper cannot report a first key. Those details cannot be inferred from a `null` result. For current behavior, examine the published notice and replay problem category rather than expecting a key name.

## Validation before replacement

`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.

`useGame.loadBoard(code)` follows the same broad shape with a board-code parser. It trims the control's draft, checks the result, and only then resets the clock and constructs a replacement game. A valid board-code string is sufficient for a fresh deal; a snapshot needs the additional position checks because it claims progress.

Failure changes visible feedback and the announcement counter. It does not replace the game, reset the running clock, save a different size or discard the edited draft. “Keeps the game” therefore does not mean that every field of the containing `Session` has reference equality: notices are session fields too. Nor does it freeze the active game while someone corrects text. A running game can continue to gain elapsed time after an unsuccessful load.

This distinction is visible in `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts`: the test enters bad board and snapshot drafts, verifies the notices and retained text, then advances the clock and verifies that the prior game is still running. A test that expected elapsed time to remain fixed indefinitely after rejection would assert behavior the product does not have.

## The shared JSON boundary

The small helpers in `src/game/saved-format.ts` separate JSON mechanics from game validation:

| Helper | Meaning at this boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `isWithinBytes(text, maxBytes)` | Measures UTF-8 encoded length, inclusively |
| `parseJson(text)` | Returns parsed unknown data, or `undefined` after a parse exception |
| `isJsonObject(value)` | Accepts non-null objects except arrays |
| `hasExactKeys(value, keys)` | Checks own-key count and presence of every expected own key |
| `isNonnegativeSafeInteger(value)` | Accepts numeric safe integers greater than or equal to zero |

`JSON.parse` can produce `null`, a list, a string, a boolean or a number. Those are valid JSON texts and invalid snapshot or replay roots. The object guard is what distinguishes them from a malformed text error. This is especially visible in replay results: `{` produces `malformedJson`, whereas `null` produces `format`.

`parseJson` does not execute input as code. A string containing script-like characters is still a string and fails where an object or number is required. The decoder does not merge the parsed object into the live session wholesale. It constructs the accepted state from a generated board and the fields it has validated.

Exact keys are checked as a set, not as an ordering constraint. Missing fields fail as well as extra fields. Nested objects are checked at their own format boundaries. A `closed` selection with an `index` is invalid even if that index would be an eligible position in a different selection variant. A replay action with an annotation field is invalid even if `atMs` and `index` are otherwise good.

The helpers operate on the parsed object, not the original token stream. JSON duplicate property names are consequently handled by `JSON.parse` before exact-key checking; the decoder does not retain a record of earlier overwritten occurrences. Likewise, numeric notation such as `1.0` becomes the number `1`. The integer predicate checks the value it receives rather than enforcing a preferred spelling of a JSON number.

## Resource bounds are checked at the text boundary

Snapshot decoding measures its input before parsing and rejects text above `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES`, which is `65_536`. Replay reading checks `REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, which is `1_048_576`, before parsing. The replay parser then rejects more than `REPLAY_MAX_ACTIONS`, which is `10_000`. Trailing JSON whitespace is legal within the byte budget and still consumes that budget.

These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.

The browser textarea's `maxLength` is a separate character limit. Multibyte text can satisfy that limit and exceed the decoder's byte limit. The existing byte helper test uses an accented character to establish that bytes, rather than JavaScript string length, control acceptance. Snapshot format discusses how this interacts with readable export text.

## Snapshot checks depend on the regenerated deal

After validating the version and board code, `decodeSnapshot` generates the board used to interpret positions. `readMatched` checks unique in-range positions and requires both copies of every represented face. An even-length list alone is not enough: on `np1-4-1`, `[2, 6]` is a pair while `[0, 1]` is not.

`readSelection` checks availability against that matched list. A mismatch needs different positions with different faces and an integer remaining interval from `1` through `800`. It cannot describe a same-face pair awaiting closure, because normal play resolves matching cards immediately. When every position is matched, availability also prevents any nonclosed selection.

The full decoder checks counter bounds, a minimum move count and consistency with `started`. These checks establish the stated constraints without reconstructing every earlier action. Snapshot format gives the complete validation sequence; Snapshot selection notes explains the board-dependent helpers.

## Replay checks and isolated evaluation

`readReplay` checks root shape, version, board code, action count and `endMs` before walking actions. Each action then needs its exact object shape, safe nonnegative numbers, a nondecreasing timestamp no later than `endMs`, and a position inside the deck. Its index into the action array is included in action-specific failures.

Evaluation can already have computed earlier actions when a later action fails. That is safe because the evolving state is local to `readReplay`; no browser session has been committed. The function returns a problem rather than that partial state. This is different from a streaming UI that visibly applies each imported action as it reads.

An in-range activation during a mismatch is valid replay data even though the game ignores it. So are an activation of an already matched card and a repeated activation of the current first card. Validation checks whether the action is well formed; `activateCard` decides whether it changes play. Treating every ignored activation as a corrupt replay would conflate these two jobs.

Action timestamps may be much larger than the elapsed clock cap. The replay evaluator advances the logical timeline using safe integers, while `advanceGame` caps the resulting elapsed counter. That distinction prevents a legitimate long timeline from being rejected merely because the visible clock has saturated. Replay format explains exact timeout edges and equal-time order.

## Failure reports that preserve the evidence

For current snapshot failures the decoder deliberately supplies no reason. The most effective local investigation isolates a single change against a known accepted object: replace just the selection, just the code, or just one counter. The tests in `snapshot.test.ts` use this pattern so that an unrelated invalid baseline cannot hide a missing check.

Replay reports have more detail. `readReplay` distinguishes file size, JSON syntax, root format, board code, actions array, end time, individual action shape, time order and index bounds. The CLI translates these into stderr text and uses a one-based action number for readers. Internal action positions remain zero-based. Mixing these conventions can lead an engineer to inspect the wrong action.

Retaining original text matters when a failure depends on bytes or syntax. Parsing and reserializing a padded document can remove the very length excess that caused its rejection. A screenshot of a notice cannot establish whether an extra property was nested or at the root. For the current accepted shapes, use Board code format, Snapshot format and Replay format; for the browser steps around them, use Sharing FAQ.
# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is Reproducibility. This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See Format versioning for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in Board code format.

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. Snapshot format gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. Replay format covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See Reproduction panel and Focus policy for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. Import safety describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.
# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. Typography and Form layout guide explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. Accessibility audit provides the wider review context.
# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. Focus policy covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. Reproduction panel documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. Clock design and Mismatch interval explain the established clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in Board keyboard navigation.

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is Native controls guide for element choice, Focus policy for page orientation and New game and restart for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.
# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. Dialog policy covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. Error display guide follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. Board keyboard navigation provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. Interface review checklist gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.
# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `<span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result | Text produced by the session |
| --- | --- |
| First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` |
| Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` |
| Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. Screen reader notes follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. Reproduction panel and Focus policy describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.
# Target size policy

This page records the control target policy and explains the size constraints already present in the interface styles.

Target size is about the area a person can activate, not the size of a glyph drawn inside it. A card's marker is small, but the native button enclosing the whole card is the target. The same distinction applies to a summary's disclosure marker and the much larger summary row.

## Policy and present coverage

The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.

The current styles are useful building blocks, but they are not proof of every dimension for an arbitrary new element. In particular, `.control` declares minimum height without a general minimum width. A new short-label action could be tall enough while still being too narrow. The policy check and the existing class definition therefore answer related but different questions.

This is a control policy, not a claim of complete accessibility conformance. The visuals specification makes the same distinction for its chosen card minimum. Names, keyboard operation, contrast, visible focus and error behavior still have their own evidence. Interface review checklist gathers those areas without turning a size measurement into a blanket result.

## Size sources in the current code

| Element | Source | Existing size behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Card button | `board.css`, `card.css` | Grid tracks from 44px to 88px, square aspect ratio |
| Button, select, input, textarea using `.control` | `control.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px |
| Reproduction summary | `reproduction.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 12px 16px |
| Deal action row | `controls.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |
| Reproduction action row | `reproduction.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |

`game.css` applies `box-sizing: border-box` globally. The declared height constraints therefore include padding and border. Looking only at text line height would underestimate the target, while adding padding to the measured border box would overestimate it.

Cards have `width: 100%`, `aspect-ratio: 1`, zero padding and a `2px` border. Their width comes from the grid track. They do not establish their minimum using the SVG's coordinates or intrinsic artwork size. The current artwork can change shape while the card target remains the same square.

## Why large boards scroll

The inner board calculates a minimum content width from side length, `--card-min` and `--card-gap`. On a sixteen-column board that is 794px before viewport padding and border. A phone cannot display that whole width at once while keeping the current card minimum.

The implementation chooses an internal scroll area. Its `overflow: auto` and `max-width: 100%` allow the board to extend inside a bounded viewport. The outer page stays within the window. This is the reason a sixteen-column board does not respond like a shrunken thumbnail of a four-column board.

A target-size review can therefore encounter two valid observations at once: every card has its intended dimensions, and some cards are outside the current visible portion of the board. Reachability is supplied by scrolling and keyboard movement. Pointer and touch explains the touch path to the last card; Board keyboard navigation explains arrow access.

A partially clipped card also has a full underlying button box. Clicking the visible part can activate it, after which the current implementation scrolls it fully into view. That behavior does not mean the clipping itself should be measured as the card's intended dimensions. It is an overflow case with a separate focus and pointer timing concern.

## Phone layout affects widths

At `max-width: 599px`, the deal size group fills the row and uses space-between alignment. New Game and Restart receive `flex: 1`. This gives the actions room without hard-coding two button widths. The text and browser control still contribute their intrinsic size constraints.

The reproduction action rows also wrap, with buttons growing on the phone breakpoint. The Board code input has `flex: 1`, a preferred width of `16ch` and `min-width: 0`. The textarea fills its parent and can resize vertically. These choices keep the text tools within the available width rather than making the outer page horizontally scroll.

A visual review at a wide desktop window can miss the consequences of a new wrapper or label. Selectors such as `.controls > button` and `.control-row > button` apply to direct children. If a wrapper changes which element grows, measuring the wrapper rather than the actual button can hide a target-width problem.

The overall content has `16px` page padding and a maximum width of `1120px`. A viewport width is therefore not the same thing as a control's available row width. Panel padding, gaps and borders consume space too. Reading the size policy as a viewport measurement alone would skip the layout where the target actually lives.

## Visible content versus activation area

A native button may contain text, a shape or multiple SVG pieces. In Card, the face SVG and matched check mark are descendants of one button, and the click callback is attached to that button. Their separate geometry does not produce separate tiny controls.

The neutral back is a `12px` span with a rotated border and `aria-hidden="true"`. It is deliberately smaller than the card. Counting its bounds as the input target would describe the drawing rather than the event-handling element. Similarly, the matched check is a state mark, not a separate action with its own click listener.

Focus outlines sit outside the control border and do not add activation area. Hover border changes likewise do not expand the target. Measurements used to assess the policy concern the actual element box; measurements used to assess focus visibility include outline width and offset. The project already has separate helpers for that distinction in `tests/focus-bounds.ts`.

The reproduction summary is another useful case. Its text and disclosure marker occupy only part of a padded native summary element. The element supplies the disclosure interaction. Replacing it with a visually similar small icon could change both target size and semantics; the current source does neither.

## Zoom, density and CSS units

The policy uses CSS pixels. Device pixel ratio affects the mapping to physical pixels, not the DOM geometry reported by `getBoundingClientRect`. A test at device scale 2 can still report a 44px CSS box. Multiplying the bounding-box result by device scale would answer a different question.

The repository's equivalent zoom layout uses a `640x400` viewport with device scale 2. It checks that controls, statistics and the completion summary remain readable and that both small and large boards remain playable. This is useful complementary evidence for a layout that wraps and scrolls rather than simply shrinking every element.

The game does not disable pinch zoom. Card touch handling uses `touch-action: manipulation`, and index.html does not impose a maximum scale. A target remains part of a browser page whose visible scale can change. Zoom behaviour covers the visual contract in more detail.

## Existing evidence and what it establishes

`tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks the default board and control dimensions at `320x640`. It measures `.controls button`, `.controls select` and `.card` boxes and checks minimum width and height. The same file checks large boards at phone and desktop viewports, where the card floor, viewport height and complete focus ring are important.

Those checks establish the existing tested elements at their stated layouts. They do not automatically cover a future control merely because it shares a color or appears next to a tested button. The source selectors and actual bounding box identify the scope of evidence.

For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.

The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. Native controls guide explains that architectural advantage, while Contrast audit and Focus policy cover other properties that a dimension alone cannot establish.
# Module layout policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs places behavior in the source tree and how to extend that structure without obscuring the game rules.

The current tree is small enough to read directly. It has no application framework around the game, no route hierarchy and no general service container. `src/main.tsx` mounts `Game`; the application then divides into rule functions, a session adapter and components for the board, controls and status. Source layout is the file inventory. This page explains the choices behind it.

## Follow behavior before file type

The board directory contains `Board.tsx`, `Card.tsx`, `Face.tsx`, navigation helpers, card descriptions, face design, styles and focused tests. Its contents answer a coherent set of questions: how a position is presented, how focus moves and how a face becomes visible. A separate top-level directory for every hook, type or stylesheet would make those questions harder to answer.

The session directory has a different responsibility. It connects rules to React state, browser observations and saved preferences. A feature lives in src/game/FEATURE/, and its rules live in src/game/FEATURE/rules.ts, which imports neither React nor any browser global. That placement gives a reader a predictable starting point for a feature's decisions, with the integration code close enough to inspect alongside them.

This convention applies to feature work; existing behaviors also use other filenames. The current core is in `game.ts`, `deck.ts`, `selection.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts` and `replay.ts` directly under `src/game`. The board already uses focused names such as `keyboard.ts` and `card-state.ts`.

## The dependency direction

The central rules know about game data. `game.ts` imports the deck generator and the selection union. It does not import `Game.tsx`, `Board.tsx` or the session hook. `snapshot.ts` rebuilds and validates a game using those same definitions. `replay.ts` applies logical advances and activations to a game without rendering it.

The session layer points inward. `session.ts` calls `activateCard`, `advanceGame`, `createGame` and `isWon`, then adds session feedback, import pause state and best-score decisions. `use-game.ts` provides callable actions to components. The UI receives values and actions; it does not become the only place where a legal turn can be computed.

There are intentional lateral imports. `storage.ts` uses `GRID_SIZES` and `MOVES_MAX` to validate preferences against actual game limits. `card-state.ts` uses `faceDesign` to describe a visible face. These relationships connect meanings that genuinely belong together. They do not form a general helpers layer with unrelated operations.

A useful way to inspect an unfamiliar change is to start at its public behavior and follow direct imports toward the core. A card click leads through the controller to `activateSession` and `activateCard`. A loaded snapshot leads through `decodeSnapshot`, `readMatched` and `readSelection`. The direction remains visible because there are no barrel files hiding which definition is used.

## State is divided by meaning

`GameState` extends the board description with matched positions, the current selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and a start flag. It does not store a focus position or a form draft. The board description includes its code, size, seed and deck. `generateBoard` freezes the description and deck at runtime, while the TypeScript interfaces expose readonly fields.

`Session` wraps that game with `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. A generation identifies a replacement deal. It is not a move count and does not belong in a snapshot. Feedback belongs here because turn results and imports need session-level presentation, while replay needs only the final game state.

The board hook owns its remembered focused index. `Reproduction` owns the textarea draft. `BoardCodeForm` uses an uncontrolled input initialized from the current code, with its generation key causing a fresh input on replacement. These values have useful local lifetimes. Moving them into `GameState` would make serialization and rule transitions depend on presentation details.

## Splitting a file

Technology specification T06 sets an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 authored TypeScript lines per file. The source audit checks the ceiling across `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `art`. The aim is a reading aid, not a reason to scatter every function into a separate module.

The current snapshot split is instructive. `snapshot.ts` owns the outer format, byte bound, numeric fields, serialization and consistency checks. `snapshot-selection.ts` owns the nested selection and matched-position interpretation. Both operate on the same domain, but their validation tasks are distinct enough to read independently. `saved-format.ts` holds the small operations actually shared by snapshot, replay and preferences.

The clock split follows a different seam. `browser-clock.ts` performs arithmetic on supplied observations. `use-session-clock.ts` owns observation, scheduling, visibility and cleanup. Splitting those by arbitrary line count would lose the reason for the boundary. Clock design follows the interaction in detail.

A file can stay short while still carrying several unrelated concerns. Conversely, a dense type and a straightforward exhaustive branch may reasonably live together. The existing architecture asks for splitting by behavior, so a review considers what a reader would need to understand together before considering the final line count.

## Imports expose the owner

The source uses static ESM imports with `.ts` and `.tsx` suffixes. Types are imported with `import type` or an inline `type` marker. `use-game.ts` imports the snapshot decoder directly from `../snapshot.ts`; it does not import an application-wide registry. `Controls.tsx` imports `GRID_SIZES` from `../deck.ts`, where supported sizes are defined.

That directness matters when a symbol changes. `SelectionKind` is the owner of the selection discriminants; both rules and validators use it. `MISMATCH_MS` is defined beside turn resolution and imported where an interval bound is needed. A second constant with the same current number would hide a semantic disagreement until a later change.

The source convention tests also inspect exported values. They look for an importer for every recognized export and a single owner for each recognized exported constant name. This is a lightweight check, not a complete module system. Its practical effect is to discourage speculative public helpers and ambiguous exported constants. Source audit notes describes the exact text patterns and their limitations.

## Components and their adjacent styles

Component imports make stylesheet ownership explicit. `Game.tsx` imports `game.css`; `Board.tsx` imports `board.css`; `Card.tsx` imports `card.css`; the controls share `control.css` and add their own layout sheets. These are global CSS files, not generated CSS modules. Adjacency helps locate a selector, but it does not automatically scope one.

A board change can therefore involve both a local sheet and root styling. `board.css` defines `.board-viewport`, whose geometry is consumed by focus scrolling. `game.css` defines the global focus outline and the page width. Reading only the nearest stylesheet is sometimes insufficient. CSS organization traces these dependencies without turning visual requirements into module rules.

## Test support and application support

`game.fixture.ts` supplies a documented example code, a literal deck, its pairs and specification vectors. Application modules do not import it. Browser support in `tests/game-fixture.ts` loads a fixed board through the reproduction controls. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements the documented shuffle with BigInt arithmetic so the browser suite can reason about deals independently.

The separate `art` entries reuse application components but remain separate builds. `art/face-sheet.tsx` renders the real card component for each face. `art/session/session-harness.tsx` mounts the game beside an unmount button so teardown can be measured. Neither entry is imported by `src/main.tsx`.

That distinction explains why a helper can be useful without belonging in the shipped game. A fixture has permission to know the complete fixed deck. A hidden card in the application receives `null` instead of its face until revealed. Moving diagnostic knowledge into runtime code would bypass that deliberate presentation boundary.

## Examples of placement decisions

A correction to arrow-key edge behavior belongs first in `board/keyboard.ts`, which computes a target index from an index, size, key and modifiers. Its React caller translates a target into DOM focus. A change to the scroll behavior belongs in the hook or `nearest-scroll.ts`, because it concerns the browser's focus and scrolling behavior.
