docs/text-entry-policy.md:5:Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:9:A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:11:The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:17:The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:25:| `O'Neil` | `O'Neil` | The apostrophe is retained |
docs/text-entry-policy.md:27:The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:31:A name can also contain multiple words. Collapsing a whitespace run does not merge words together; it leaves a separating space. Treating the policy as “delete all whitespace” would change `Ada Lovelace` into a different string and would not implement the stated behavior.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:35:A draft is what someone is still editing. A stored value is what an action has accepted. The policy determines the representation of accepted and displayed names, but it does not prescribe that the caret jump after every keystroke or that an input method's partial composition be rewritten while it is active.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:37:That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:39:The current Reproduction component provides a useful example of draft ownership, though its data is not a name. Its snapshot string lives in local React state and is sent to the decoder on Load snapshot. BoardCodeForm instead reads its native form field at submission. Either storage approach can host an input boundary; the choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:45:The Board code input is a native text input with `maxLength={32}`, spell checking disabled and autocomplete off. On submission, `use-game.ts` calls `code.trim()` before `parseBoardCode(code)`. That is the only cleanup in that loading path.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:47:The grammar is a version prefix, supported side length and seed separated by hyphens. For example, surrounding spaces around `np1-6-1` are accepted by the control, but an internal space changes the grammar and is rejected. The loader does not collapse arbitrary interior text or repair the seed.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:51:Board-code parsing is also available as a core function. Calling `parseBoardCode` directly is not the same as passing through the UI loader's trim step. When reading a failure report, the entry point matters. A format parser and an input adapter can have distinct responsibilities without the application guessing what malformed identifiers meant.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:57:Applying name cleanup to the entire JSON draft would conflate two kinds of input. Whitespace can occur between tokens or inside a JSON string, with different meanings. The existing code passes the complete draft to `decodeSnapshot`; it does not first treat it as display prose or a person's name.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:59:The same is true for error preservation. On malformed JSON, the text remains editable and the current game remains present. That behavior supports correction of a structured draft. Accepted names use the normalized representation described above.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:65:Canonical equivalence is easiest to miss when examples are written as visually identical letters. A composed accented character and a base character followed by a combining mark may render alike while having different underlying sequences. A useful representation check includes both forms and inspects the accepted value rather than only its screenshot.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:67:The policy also leaves capitalization alone at this representation step. A comparison operation may have its own policy, but that does not require changing a person's displayed capitalization. Keeping display representation and comparison purpose distinct avoids presenting a comparison key as someone's chosen name.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:69:Likewise, a font's treatment of a character does not change the text stored. A missing glyph, a ligature or a different script's shaping belongs to rendering and typography. The representation policy can be implemented correctly while a layout still needs work to display the name legibly. Typography provides the visual context.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:71:The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:75:There are no name-specific tests in the repository because no name entry has been implemented. The useful evidence for a future implementation would connect its draft, accepted model and displayed text using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:77:Repeated processing should not progressively change the accepted spelling. The transformations described here have a stable result once applied. If editing, saving and displaying the same accepted name repeatedly removes more content each time, that points to an implementation doing more than the stated representation work.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:79:The current code's strongest relevant lesson is explicit boundaries: BoardCodeForm submits a draft, the controller validates, replacement updates the model, and rendered controls follow that model. Names need their own representation boundary within the feature that introduces them. The present board-code and snapshot controls use their own input boundaries.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:7:The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:9:Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes ADR 011. The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:13:The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:15:The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:19:`PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:21:The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. Preferences store and Storage failure policy describe the existing behavior.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:25:Renaming every key at once would make the storage inspector look uniform, but would create work and risk unrelated to the new naming need. Continuing the original dotted pattern indefinitely would avoid any new convention while leaving this replacement decision without effect. The selected approach separates continuity for existing data from a clear naming choice for additions.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:27:A single giant application value could avoid choosing new keys at all. That would couple unrelated data families to the same read, validation and write path. The current preferences envelope is appropriately small for size and best moves.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:31:The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:33:The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. Persistence envelope, Format versioning guide and ADR 053 explain the surrounding boundaries.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:37:## The current preferences key and value shape
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:39:These are the existing declarations. The new naming decision preserves this identifier rather than silently changing where the application reads its preferences.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:5:The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:9:The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from Text entry policy. Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:11:The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:13:The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:19:A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:21:The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:23:The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:29:| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:31:| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:32:| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:33:| `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited |
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:35:These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; Name length policy covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:37:A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:41:A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:45:The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. Error display guide provides the current feedback mechanics.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:49:Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:51:Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:53:For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:5:Browser storage contains strings outside the type system. A value may have been written by an older build, edited by a person, truncated by a debugging experiment or replaced by another script on the origin. The current preference reader accepts only a usable preference aggregate and otherwise returns its default. It does not try to repair individual score entries.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:9:A failed decode produces empty application data rather than a partially interpreted value. The read path can abandon unusable content without deleting the browser string as part of that read. A stored value that fails to parse or validate is treated as empty, without any error, and stays untouched until the next save replaces it. The distinction between reading and saving matters because a save can follow immediately during application initialization.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:11:For current preferences, “empty” is the complete fallback `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }`. `DEFAULT_SIZE` is 4. The result is therefore a fresh default-size game with no known bests, rather than an empty board or a blocked screen. `readPreferences` makes that fallback before entering its `try` block and returns it from each rejection branch.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:13:The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:17:`parseJson` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` catches `JSON.parse` errors and returns `undefined`. A string such as `{` therefore fails without throwing an uncaught exception from the preference reader. Valid JSON can still be unusable: `null`, an array, a string, a boolean or a number does not provide the required preference object.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:19:`isJsonObject` rejects null and arrays. After that narrowing, the reader checks `schemaVersion === PREFERENCES_VERSION` and requires `size` to have JavaScript type `number`. It then checks that size against `isValidSize` and requires `bestMoves` to be an object. A string value such as `"6"` is not accepted as a selected size even though the UI select ultimately uses string option values.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:21:The empty string is handled even earlier. `if (!text) return fallback` covers a missing key returned as `null`, an empty stored string and a null store's absent result. It avoids parsing text that cannot represent the preference object. Whitespace-only text is truthy, reaches the parser and fails there.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:23:These branches are worth keeping separate in a test log. They converge on the same application state, but one shows absent data, another shows malformed syntax and another shows a structural mismatch. No error copy is rendered for these preference cases.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:27:The reader builds a fresh `bestMoves` object and iterates through `Object.entries(value.bestMoves)`. For each entry it converts the key with `Number(size)`, then compares `String(numberSize)` with the original key. That round trip requires the canonical size spelling. It rejects `04`, `4.0`, `4e0` and strings padded with whitespace, even when numerical conversion would produce 4.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:29:The numeric key must then be supported by `isValidSize`. Each move count must be a nonnegative safe integer, no greater than `MOVES_MAX`, and no smaller than the number of pairs for its size. `MOVES_MAX` is 999999. The lower bound is `numberSize ** 2 / 2`, because completing the board takes at least one move for each pair.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:41:A failure at any entry returns the fallback for the entire preference value. A valid selected size of 6 does not survive alongside an invalid 4x4 score of 1. Likewise, valid score entries are not salvaged around one bad entry. The local object being assembled is never returned on that failure path.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:71:All four produce the same preference fallback. The reader does not emit different messages or a machine-readable rejection reason. A diagnostic harness can identify the failed condition by choosing one changed field at a time. The production API does not expose those distinctions to components.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:79:The 4x4 record is retained, the board starts at 6x6, and the 6x6 best display is `none`. Absence of a current-size best is not evidence of corruption.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:83:The preference reader does not enforce an exact property count at the top level. A value with valid expected fields and an additional property can be accepted. The returned application value includes only the selected size and the newly built score map. A normal subsequent write serializes those known fields and the schema discriminator, omitting the extra property.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:85:This is different from the snapshot parser, which rejects unknown fields according to its own format. A shared JSON helper does not make all parsers equally strict. Tests that copy a snapshot rejection case into preferences without checking the reader could accidentally demand behavior the game does not implement.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:87:The current reader also does not coerce score strings to numbers, round fractions or clamp out-of-range scores. A value of `"8"` is not accepted as a move count. A fraction is rejected rather than rounded. A number above the move cap invalidates the aggregate rather than being reduced to the cap. Validation produces a known state or the fallback, not a best-effort approximation of the edited input.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:89:## The timeline of replacement
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:93:In the browser, those latter two stages are separated by React's render and effect cycle rather than by a player's explicit action. `useGame` initializes session state from the read result, then `useSavedPreferences` writes that state after mounting. A test inspecting storage only after the UI has settled can see valid defaults and miss the original corrupt text entirely.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:95:The simplest way to prove read nonmutation is a store double whose `setItem` records calls. Invoke only `readPreferences`, inspect the original string and check that no write occurred. A separate browser test can demonstrate mount replacement. Combining both assertions into a single post-navigation observation loses the distinction this policy depends on.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:99:Invalid input typed into the board-code and snapshot controls follows another interaction. Those controls keep the current game, preserve the draft for correction and show their defined validation status. They do not silently replace the active game with a default board. That feedback is appropriate because the person has just requested an explicit load operation.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:103:None of these parsers establishes authenticity. A manually edited score of 8 for 4x4 is accepted if the surrounding value is valid, even without evidence that eight pairs were played. The constraints establish a plausible stored aggregate, not a verified score history.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:107:`storage.test.ts` already covers malformed JSON, null, an empty object, unsupported size, scores below the pair count, negative and fractional values, and a noncanonical key. It separately checks that a score at the move cap round-trips and one beyond it is rejected. The browser persistence contract test seeds malformed text before navigation and checks for a playable 16-card default board.
docs/corrupt-data-policy.md:109:Those tests are focused evidence, not an exhaustive enumeration of every possible JSON string. A new bug report is easiest to isolate with its exact raw value and one field changed at a time. Comparing an independently written valid baseline with the failing value exposes whether the issue concerns syntax, object shape, selected size, key spelling or score bounds. Storage testing guide gives the browser setup and store doubles for doing that without modifying the source.
docs/dialog-policy.md:5:The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.
docs/dialog-policy.md:7:## The confirmation boundary
docs/dialog-policy.md:9:A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.
docs/dialog-policy.md:11:There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.
docs/dialog-policy.md:13:The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. Focus policy covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.
docs/dialog-policy.md:17:`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.
docs/dialog-policy.md:21:The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. Reproduction panel documents the actual disclosure.
docs/dialog-policy.md:23:This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.
docs/dialog-policy.md:27:The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.
docs/dialog-policy.md:29:Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.
docs/dialog-policy.md:31:The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.
docs/dialog-policy.md:33:No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.
docs/dialog-policy.md:37:A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.
docs/dialog-policy.md:39:Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. Clock design and Mismatch interval explain the established clock model.
docs/dialog-policy.md:41:Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.
docs/dialog-policy.md:43:The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.
docs/dialog-policy.md:47:Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.
docs/dialog-policy.md:51:A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.
docs/dialog-policy.md:53:The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in Board keyboard navigation.
docs/dialog-policy.md:57:The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.
docs/dialog-policy.md:59:A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.
docs/dialog-policy.md:63:The relevant background is Native controls guide for element choice, Focus policy for page orientation and New game and restart for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.

5:The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences.
9:A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board.
11:For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other.
17:`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values.
25:  "bestMoves": {
32:There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.
34:The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history.
36:Preferences store and best score records explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format.
42:The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object.
44:Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game.
46:There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller.
52:Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize.
54:The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.
56:`rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. Persistence overview and React boundaries cover those existing responsibilities.
60:The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best.
62:That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path.
64:`src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot.
68:Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8.
70:The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result.
